unit-m21.title: Topic 2 · 2-1 Mental Math: Add and Subtract

summary.text: Lesson 2-1 of enVision Math Grade 4: adding and subtracting mentally by reshaping numbers first — breaking apart by place value, compensation with a fix-up, counting up when numbers are close, and reordering addends with the Commutative and Associative Properties.

why.text: Mental math is the first thing Topic 2 builds because everything after it — estimating, checking the algorithm — leans on being able to move numbers around in your head. It is also the skill you will actually use at a store, not the algorithm.

objectives.text: Add and subtract mentally using break apart, compensation, and counting up
Use the Commutative and Associative Properties to reorder addends
Pick the strategy that fits the numbers, and say why
Explain which way a compensation fix-up must go

parentNote.text: Built from the Topic 2 textbook scan, Lesson 2-1. The one thing to watch: the fix-up direction in compensation. Rounding a number UP before adding means SUBTRACTING the extra at the end — two questions target exactly that flip because it is the error the lesson itself warns about. Everything here is meant to be done without paper.

nextUp.text: Cards first, then the quiz in one sitting — and genuinely no paper. That is the point.

cards.def:
**Some additions and subtractions are faster in your head than on paper — if you reshape the numbers first.**
• The three big reshaping tools: break apart, compensation, counting up.
• The reshaping is the skill. The adding at the end should feel easy.

**Split one number by place value and add the pieces one at a time.**
• 3,450 + 2,380: add 2,000, then 300, then 80 — landing on 5,830.
• Each step is a one-place addition your head can hold.
cards.hint: Peel the second number like an onion: thousands layer, hundreds layer, tens layer.

cards.def:
**Trade a number for a friendlier one, then fix the answer by exactly what the trade changed.**
• 4,999 + 2,375: use 5,000, get 7,375, take the borrowed 1 back — 7,374.
• The fix-up UNDOES the trade. If the trade added, the fix-up subtracts.
cards.hint: Borrowed amounts always get returned. Compensation is honest bookkeeping.

cards.def:
**When the two numbers in a subtraction are close, walk from the smaller up to the larger and add your steps.**
• 3,004 − 2,997: 3 steps to reach 3,000, then 4 more — the difference is 7.
• No regrouping, no algorithm, just two small hops.

**Addends can swap order (Commutative Property) and regroup (Associative Property) — the sum never changes.**
• 47 + 38 + 53: pair 47 + 53 = 100 first, then add 38 — 138.
• Hunt the ones digits for pairs that make ten.

questions.q: Add 4,999 + 2,375 in your head. What is the sum?
questions.hint: Trade 4,999 for a friendlier number first.
steps: Trade 4,999 for 5,000 — that slips 1 extra into the sum.
Take the borrowed 1 back: 7,374.

ex.main: **7,374.** Compensation: compute with 5,000, then return the 1 you borrowed.
ex.tip: The fix-up always undoes exactly what the trade did — nothing more, nothing less.

questions.q: To add 47 + 38 + 53 in your head, which first move makes it easiest?
opts: Pair 47 and 53 to make 100, then add 38
Add 47 and 38 first because they come first
Round every number to the nearest ten and add the rounds
Add all the ones digits, then start over with the tens
questions.hint: Look for two ones digits that make ten.
steps: Scan for a friendly pair: 47 + 53 = 100.
Addends may be reordered and regrouped freely — the sum cannot change.
100 + 38 = 138, done in one breath.

ex.main: **Pair 47 and 53 — they make 100.** Order never matters in addition, so pick the order that helps.
ex.tip: The tell is in the ones digits: 7 and 3 make ten. Train your eye to spot those pairs.

questions.hint: Trade 398 for a rounder number, then settle up.
steps: Subtracting 400 took away 2 too many.
Give the 2 back: 302.

ex.main: **302.** Taking away 400 overshoots by 2, so the answer collects them back.
ex.tip: When you round the number being subtracted UP, your first answer is too SMALL. Push it back up.

questions.q: Compute 6,000 − 1,998 mentally. What is the difference?
questions.hint: Which way does the fix-up go after trading 1,998 for 2,000?
steps: 2,000 is 2 more than the problem asked you to remove.
You took 2 too many, so hand them back: 4,002.

ex.main: **4,002.** The trade removed 2 extra, and the fix-up returns exactly those 2.
ex.tip: Say the direction out loud: "I subtracted too much, so I add back." That sentence prevents the classic flip.

questions.q: Which subtraction is the best fit for counting UP instead of the written algorithm?
questions.hint: Counting up shines when the gap is small.
steps: Counting up means walking from the smaller number to the larger one.
3,004 and 2,997 are only a few apart: 3 to reach 3,000, then 4 more — 7.
The other pairs are thousands apart; walking that far defeats the point.

ex.main: **3,004 − 2,997.** The gap is tiny, so two easy hops finish it.
ex.tip: Close numbers: count up. Far-apart numbers: break apart, compensate, or use the algorithm.

questions.q: A library adds 3,450 books one year and 2,380 the next. Break 2,380 apart by place value to find the total mentally.
questions.hint: Add the thousands, then the hundreds, then the tens.
steps: Start at 3,450. Add the thousands: 3,450 + 2,000 = 5,450.
Add the hundreds: 5,450 + 300 = 5,750.

ex.main: **5,830.** Break apart turns one hard addition into three easy ones.
ex.tip: Each step touches one place value. If a step feels hard, you broke the number apart too coarsely.

questions.hint: The numbers are close together — walk between them.
steps: Count up from 7,985.

ex.main: **18.** Two short hops: 15 to reach the round number, 3 to finish.
ex.tip: Aim your first hop at the nearest round number — it splits the walk into pieces you can hold.

questions.q: To add 1,985 + 2,595, Elena trades 1,985 for 2,000, gets 2,000 + 2,595 = 4,595, then ADDS 15 more for a final answer of 4,610. Judge her work.
opts: Her trade was fine, but the fix-up runs the other way — the sum is 4,580
She should have traded 2,595 for 2,600 so no fix-up is needed
Compensation cannot be used on four-digit numbers
questions.hint: Did her trade make the running total too big or too small?
steps: Trading 1,985 up to 2,000 slipped an extra 15 INTO the sum.
The fix-up must take that 15 back out: 4,595 − 15 = 4,580.
Elena added 15 again instead, landing 30 too high at 4,610.
The fix-up UNDOES the trade — it never repeats it.

ex.main: **The fix-up runs backwards — 4,580.** She padded the sum by 15 with the trade, then padded it again.
ex.tip: After any trade, ask one question: did that make my answer too big or too small? Then push it back.

questions.q: Maya computes 5,996 + 3,477 as 6,000 + 3,477 − 4. Jae computes it as 6,000 + 3,473. Who gets the right answer?
opts: Both — each removed exactly the 4 that the trade added
Only Maya — the fix-up must come at the end
Only Jae — the fix-up must come before adding
Neither — trading changes the sum for good
questions.hint: Track the extra 4. Does each method get rid of it once?
steps: Trading 5,996 for 6,000 adds a 4 that was never there.
Maya removes it after adding: 9,477 − 4 = 9,473.
Jae removes it from the other addend first: 3,477 − 4 = 3,473, then 6,000 + 3,473 = 9,473.
Same 4, removed exactly once each way — both land on 9,473.

ex.main: **Both — 9,473 either way.** The extra 4 has to leave once; when it leaves is a matter of taste.
ex.tip: Moving an amount from one addend to the other never changes a sum. That sentence IS compensation.

questions.q: Why does the trick 700 − 398 = 700 − 400 + 2 actually work?
opts: Subtracting 400 removes 2 more than asked, and adding 2 puts back exactly that overshoot
Because 398 rounds to 400, and rounded answers always agree
Because addition and subtraction are the same operation
It only works when the answer ends in 2
questions.hint: Compare what was asked with what was actually removed.
steps: The problem asks you to remove 398.
You removed 400 instead — that digs exactly 2 too deep.
Adding 2 refills exactly that hole, no more.
Every borrowed amount gets returned; the trick is bookkeeping, not magic.

ex.main: **The overshoot is exactly 2, and the +2 repairs exactly that.** Compensation always balances its books.
ex.tip: If you can say WHERE the fix-up number comes from, you own the strategy instead of memorizing it.
